citeAs: Zayene, M., Endres, J., Havolli, A., Corbière, C., Cherkaoui, S., Kontouli, A., Alahi, A. (2025). HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv:2411.18335.
creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi (EPFL, Switzerland)
description: HELVIPAD is a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames (39,553 labeled frames) from 29 video sequences across diverse indoor and outdoor environments on a university campus, under varied lighting conditions including day and night. Data were collected using two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline and a synchronized Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, providing accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images at 1920×512 resolution.
name: HELVIPAD
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Projection accuracy was assessed by calculating pixel error as Euclidean distances between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions, resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels. For visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges), the error remains at 8.0 pixels. The overall average pixel error across all sequences is 8.0 pixels, corresponding to a relative error of 0.40% of the image diagonal.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels are generated automatically by projecting LiDAR point clouds onto equirectangular images. The projection uses optimized rotation and translation parameters (minimized via BFGS) to align LiDAR points with camera images. Disparity values are derived from depth values using the spherical disparity formula. Each test sequence was manually reviewed to ensure no overlap of scenes or areas with the train set.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is collected on a single university campus, which may not represent all urban environments. Night outdoor scenes are underrepresented (2 train sequences, 1 test sequence). Depth completion increases density of low-range depth values (0–10m range), enriching representation of closer objects. Indoor sequences exhibit more rapid decline in pixel percentage beyond 10 meters compared to outdoor scenes.
rai:dataCollection: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor (64 beams, 42.4° vertical FOV, 10 fps), mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. The rig was mounted on a custom-built remotely controlled robot chassis navigating a university campus across indoor (corridors, halls) and outdoor (squares, parking, footpaths) scenes under various lighting and weather conditions.
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: LiDAR point clouds are sparse compared to high-resolution camera images, covering only ~12% of pixels. Sky areas and regions with insufficient nearby LiDAR measurements are excluded from depth labels. The LiDAR's limited vertical field of view (42.4°) means only pixels within the LiDAR's field of view can be labeled.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of equirectangular video frames at 3840×1920 pixels captured at 30 fps by two Ricoh Theta V cameras, and LiDAR point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 sensor operating at 10 fps with 64 beams. The cameras and LiDAR are synchronized using a hardware-triggered flash synchronization method.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is collected on a single university campus, limiting scene diversity. The depth completion approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. Occlusions between LiDAR and cameras were not explicitly handled. The LiDAR's vertical field of view (42.4°) limits depth label coverage. Night outdoor scenes are underrepresented. Indoor-trained models show limited generalization to outdoor scenes, particularly at night.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: An augmented training set is created via a depth completion pipeline: LiDAR point clouds from 4 preceding and 4 succeeding frames are temporally aggregated, then depth is interpolated on spherical grid points using k-nearest neighbors (k=17) weighted averaging, followed by filtering of high-uncertainty and out-of-distribution points. This increases the ratio of labeled pixels from ~12% to ~61%. Photometric data augmentation is also applied during model training.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Camera frames are downsampled from 30 fps to 10 fps (retaining one out of every three frames) to match the LiDAR frame rate. Images are cropped to remove unnecessary borders (sky, ground) and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 pixels. LiDAR point clouds are projected onto equirectangular images via an optimized rotation and translation transformation (minimizing reprojection error using BFGS). Depth values are converted to spherical disparity in degrees.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset supports development of depth estimation for mobile robots used in real-world applications such as autonomous driving, healthcare, and agriculture, where accurate 3D representations of dynamic human environments are crucial for navigation and interaction.
rai:dataUseCases: Developing and benchmarking omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models; robotic navigation in dynamic human environments; assessing robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges; cross-scene generalization evaluation.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: BFGS optimization algorithm (for LiDAR-to-image projection parameter optimization); KISS-ICP (LiDAR odometry, evaluated but not used in final pipeline); automated depth completion pipeline using k-nearest neighbor interpolation on spherical grid points with temporal aggregation.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains images of pedestrians in public spaces (indoor corridors, halls, outdoor squares, footpaths, parking areas). The sequences include counts of pedestrians, with an average of 13.33 pedestrians in indoor sequences and 17.65 pedestrians in outdoor sequences.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: Labels are generated automatically from LiDAR projection; no concept of multiple independent annotations per item is discussed.
null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations are generated automatically from LiDAR sensor data; no human annotators are involved.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Annotations are generated automatically via LiDAR projection pipeline; no annotation platform is used.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation of missing values is described; depth completion is a data augmentation technique, not imputation of missing dataset values.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.

evidence.name: We introduce HELVIPAD , a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames from video sequences across diverse environments
evidence.description: It consists of 29 video sequences captured in dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes across a university campus (Fig. 1), under diverse weather and lighting conditions. Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two omnidirectional cameras in a vertical arrangement, which prevents occlusion, and paired with a synchronized LiDAR sensor to provide high-quality depth measurements.

evidence.isLiveDataset: With a total of 39,553 labeled frames, H ELVIPAD serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking omnidirectional depth estimation models capable of navigating in human environments.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: The rig features two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with a Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor with a vertical field of view of 42.4°, operating at 10 fps, and mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization. In total, we collected 29 video sequences.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The H ELVIPAD dataset includes 26 video sequences captured between December 2023 and February 2024., recorded at a frame rate of 10 Hz.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two omnidirectional cameras in a vertical arrangement, which prevents occlusion, and paired with a synchronized LiDAR sensor to provide high-quality depth measurements.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The system integrates two Ricoh Theta V cameras, which capture images in 4K/UHD equirectangular format at 30 fps with an initial resolution of 3840 × 1920 pixels. It also includes an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, operating at 10 fp with 64 beams and a vertical field of view of 42.4°.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Top images, bottom images, depth maps, and disparity maps are then cropped to remove unnecessary borders and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 to enable more efficient training. To match the LiDAR's frame rate (10 fps), we retain one out of every three camera frames.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Applying depth completion, we augment training data with a significantly increased label density, which proves to be an effective data augmentation technique for multiple models in our experiment. Applied on the H ELVIPAD dataset, our pipeline significantly increases the ratio of labeled pixels from 12% to 61% while maintaining very low error rates.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images. Each test sequence has been manually reviewed to ensure no overlap of scenes or areas with the train set.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: we calculated the pixel error by measuring Euclidean distances between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions, resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels. When selecting the same number of points from visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges), the error remains relatively low at 8.0 pixels, further confirming calibration quality.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: The core step of the mapping process is the optimization of the rotation and translation parameters, achieved by minimizing the error between the projected points and their corresponding location on the equirectangular images. KISS-ICP [33] is one of the state-of-the-art approaches for LiDAR odometry. It is based on the ICP algorithm and creates a local map of the environment.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: With a total of 39,553 labeled frames, H ELVIPAD serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking omnidirectional depth estimation models capable of navigating in human environments. This dataset is an ideal testbed for assessing the robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Mobile robots are increasingly used in real-world applications such as autonomous driving, healthcare, or agriculture, where accurate 3D representations of dynamic human environments are crucial for navigation and interaction.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Note that this approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. Occlusions were not explicitly handled, as the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact.
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: the dynamic nature of the recorded scenes is emphasized by the presence of pedestrians, with an average of 13.33 pedestrians in indoor sequences and 17.65 pedestrians in outdoor sequences.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: When comparing the depth distributions in the training set before and after depth completion, we observe that depth completion increases the density of low-range depth values, particularly within the 0–10 meter range. This shift is likely a result of the algorithm interpolating missing values and removing out-of-distribution samples. This process tends to enrich the representation of closer objects in the dataset.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Given the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images, ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels. Additionally, to avoid labeling regions with insufficient nearby points (e.g., sky areas), we compute the average distance to the k nearest neighbors for each query point
